_comment: Hindu expansion 175-drive H: Mahabharata forest tales, ascents and later-book episodes (Ganguli 1883-96, public domain).

title.en: King Sibi Weighs His Flesh Against a Dove

region.zh: 尸毗都城（象徵性定位，西北）

texts.period: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vana Parva, the story of Sibi

summary.en: A dove fleeing a hawk fell into King Sibi's lap and begged protection; the hawk, cheated of its lawful prey, demanded its dinner. The king cut flesh from his own body to weigh against the dove - more and more, until he climbed onto the scale himself. The hawk was Indra and the dove Agni, testing the most generous king on earth.
summary.zh: 一鴿逃避獵鷹，落入尸毗王懷中求庇；鷹因失去合法獵物而索其晚餐。王自體割肉以秤鴿——愈割愈多，直至親自登上秤盤。鷹即因陀羅，鴿即阿耆尼，試探世上最慷慨的王。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (also a Buddhist Jataka); classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The dove dropped into the king's lap like a falling leaf, and its voice was a voice: protect me, king; the hawk's claim is hunger, but my claim is shelter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sibi's scale was exact: he cut his own thigh to equal the dove's weight - and the dove grew heavier with every cut, as if fed by the king's giving.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last he sat himself into the pan - and the gods dropped their disguises: the test of the most generous king on earth had weighed his whole self, and found it enough; his wounds healed as the flowers fell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

region.zh: 溫迪亞山脈（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Mahabharata, Vana Parva; Purana tellings (Ganguli translation, 1883-96; Wilson 1840)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vana Parva, Agastya sections

summary.en: The Vindhya, jealous of Meru's height, grew until it blocked the sun's road: the south lived in shadow. Agastya, the dwarf seer journeying south, was asked by the mountain to pass over it; the sage asked in turn that it bow till he returned from the south - and he never returned. The mountain still waits, and the sun still passes.
summary.zh: 溫迪亞山妒於須彌之高，不斷生長直至遮斷日路：南方活在陰影之中。南行的矮小仙人阿竭多受山之請求從其上越過；仙人反請山俯首直到他自南方歸來——而他再未北返。山至今仍在等待，太陽至今仍在通行。

passages.text: The mountain grew to rival Meru, higher and higher, until the sun's road bent around it and the lands of the south lay in permanent shade.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata/Purana Agastya material (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Agastya came walking south and honored the obstacle: great one, bow till I cross; I shall return by this road - and the mountain, proud of its courtesy to a seer, folded down to the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata/Purana Agastya material (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The sage settled in the south and never took the northward road; the Vindhya keeps its bow, and the geography of two halves of India - sunlit south, waiting mountain - is one seer's promise, kept.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata/Purana Agastya material (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

region.zh: 印度洋（象徵性定位於羅摩梭瓦蘭）

texts.period: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vana Parva, the drinking of the ocean

summary.en: The Asuras Kalakeya had hidden in the ocean and raided the worlds from it; the gods came to Agastya, the seer whose appetite was his ancestor's gift. He knelt at the shore and drank the sea dry in three draughts - and the demons, standing on dry sand, were destroyed. The ocean's basin, one story says, is still the shape of that meal.
summary.zh: 迦羅迦耶群魔藏於海中，自海上襲擊世界；諸神來找阿竭多——那位以食欲為家傳的仙人。他跪於岸邊，三口飲乾滄海——群魔立足於乾沙之上，遂被誅滅。據一說，大洋的盆形至今仍是那頓飯的形狀。

passages.text: The demons' fortress was the sea itself: no army could reach the Kalakeyas in the deep, and every raid ended with their retreat into the water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Agastya came to the shore, bowed to the ocean as to a host, and drank it - the whole weight of the sea taken into a body the size of a dwarf, three draughts and the bed lay dry.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The exposed demons were cut down in the open; the gods crowned the seer, and the aition stood: why the ocean laps in a basin of that size - the appetite of the south's first sage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ramopakhyana: Rama's Story Told in the Mahabharata
title.zh: 羅摩傳：摩訶婆羅多中所講的羅摩故事

region.zh: 摩根德耶仙居（象徵性定位於尼彌沙）

texts.period: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ramopakhyana), composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vana Parva, Ramopakhyana

summary.en: Inside the Mahabharata, the sage Markandeya tells Draupadi the story of Rama: a wronged queen in exile finds hope in the epic of another exile - Rama, who won Sita back through forest, alliance and war. The Ramopakhyana is the tradition's own evidence that the two epics read each other: a Mahabharata woman comforted by a Ramayana plot.
summary.zh: 在《摩訶婆羅多》內部，仙人摩根德耶向黑公主講述羅摩的故事：一位受屈的王后在流亡中於另一流亡者的史詩裡找到希望——羅摩，經森林、結盟與戰爭而贏回悉多。《羅摩傳》是傳統自身展示兩部史詩互讀的證據：一位《摩訶婆羅多》的女子被《羅摩衍那》的情節安慰。

passages.text: Draupadi, in the forest, asked Markandeya whether any woman had ever suffered what she suffered; the sage answered with a whole epic in brief - Rama's.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Ramopakhyana (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The summary compresses the Ramayana to its skeleton: the exile, the abduction, the monkey-ally, the bridge, the war, the trial - a story shaped to console a queen that her own epic had abandoned in a forest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Ramopakhyana (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The embedded telling is textual gold: two epics quoting each other in the same mouth, a century or more before either reached its final form - the tradition's own first comparative literature.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Ramopakhyana (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

title.en: Shuka's Ascension: The Sage Who Left Through the Sky
title.zh: 叔迦的升天：自天而出走的仙人

region.zh: 叔迦仙居（象徵性定位於俱盧之野）

texts.period: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Shanti Parva, Shuka's ascent

summary.en: Vyasa's son Shuka asked the one question his father's wisdom could not dodge: what lies beyond everything? The father sent him through a curriculum - kings, sages, women, heaven's own court - and each teacher returned the same answer in a new voice. Shuka's body rose from the earth into the sky and dissolved there: the epic's own account of a soul leaving through the crown of the head.
summary.zh: 毗耶娑之子叔迦問出一個父親的智慧無法迴避的問題：萬物之外是什麼？父親遣他完成一門課程——君王、仙人、女子、天廷——每位教師以新的聲音給出同一答案。叔迦之身自大地升入天空並於彼消融：史詩自身關於靈魂自頭頂出走的敘述。

passages.text: Shuka's question was final: father, what is beyond the beyond? Vyasa, out-argued at last by his own son, sent him to ask everyone - the answer, he said, must be earned in every voice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Shanti Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The syllabus ran from Janaka's court to heaven's gate: kings and renouncers, women of wisdom and the gods themselves - and every teacher, asked about the beyond, answered with the Self.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Shanti Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: His ascension is described like weather: the body rose from the hermitage, the earth lost its hold, and the sage went out through the crown like a flame joining flame - the epic's witness to its own meaning's exit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Shanti Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

title.en: Vidura's Last Teaching and Death by Yoga
title.zh: 維杜羅的最後教導與瑜伽之死

region.zh: 俱盧之野一帶（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Mahabharata, Shanti/Anushasana Parvas, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vidura's death

summary.en: Vidura, the palace's honest conscience, came out of retirement to teach Yudhishthira the final lessons of the dead - and died as he taught: fixed in yoga under a tree, his breath leaving upward, witnessed by the king he had warned all his life. The uncle who could not save the kingdom at least died in the posture of a man who had nothing left to lose.
summary.zh: 王廷中誠實的良知維杜羅走出退休，向堅戰傳授亡者的最後課程——並於授課中死去：瑜伽定於樹下，氣息向上而出，由他一生警告過的王親眼見證。這位無法拯救王國的伯父，至少以一無所失者的姿勢死去。

passages.text: Vidura's last visit was a syllabus of warnings repeated too late: on dharma in defeat, on grief, on the self's path - the counsel of the only Kaurava who never wanted the war.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Under a banyan in the ashram he sat in yoga with the king before him; the breath was drawn up through the spine, the body cooled in place - death as the final lesson, performed rather than described.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Yudhishthira saw the truth of the death without horror: the uncle who had warned against every dice and every war died owning nothing and owing nothing - the epic's cleanest exit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

region.zh: 怛叉始羅方向（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Sambhava/Aranya sections), composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Adi Parva, Parikshit and Takshaka

summary.en: The orphaned heir of the Pandavas, cursed by a seer's boy for a fruitless disrespect, was given seven days to live by the serpent-king Takshaka. He sealed himself in a tower of guards - and Takshaka came disguised as a worm in a fruit, took his true form in the king's sight, and closed the account. His son's revenge-sacrifice opens the epic itself.
summary.zh: 般度族孤兒繼承人因一場無意的輕慢觸怒仙人之子，被蛇王多剎迦給予七天之壽。他自封於守衛環繞的高塔——多剎迦化為果中之蟲潛入，於王眼前現出真身，閉合賬目。其子的復仇之祭開啟了史詩本身。

passages.text: The seer's son, ignored in the king's court, cursed through his brother's mouth: on the seventh day from this, Takshaka shall bite thee.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The tower was sealed against every crawling thing - and the serpent-king bribed the envoys, arrived inside a fruit as a shining worm, and stood before the king in his own body with the days counted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The bite was the epic's first death: the crown passed to Janamejaya, whose snake-sacrifice - and the brahmin boy who stopped it - is where the Mahabharata begins to be recited.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

region.zh: 波希王廷，冥界（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Astika Upaparva), composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Adi Parva, Uttanka episode

summary.en: The seer's pupil Uttanka was asked, as a fee, for the divine earrings of a queen - which Takshaka's snakes had hidden in the netherworld. He rode with a blind man and an old woman who proved to be Indra and the Earth, dived into the serpent realm, charmed the snakes with a talking fire, and returned the earrings in time for the queen's vow - the epic's shortest quest, with Indra heckling from the roadside.
summary.zh: 仙人弟子鄔丹迦被索求王后之神聖耳環為學資——而多剎迦的蛇族已將其藏入冥界。他與盲者及老婦同乘（二人實為因陀羅與大地），潛入蛇域，以會言之火魅蛇，及時送回耳環——史詩中最短的探索之旅，因陀羅於路旁不斷戲弄。

passages.text: The fee was absurd on purpose: the queen's divine ear-rings, kept in the netherworld by Takshaka's snakes - a teacher's test that doubles as a treasure-hunt.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Uttanka section (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the road Indra rode with him disguised - an old man on an ass, heckling the pupil with tests of hunger and trust - and the Earth herself lent the route; the underworld gate opened to a boy who knew its word.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Uttanka section (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the serpent city the earrings were recovered with the help of a fire that spoke; Uttanka returned in time for the queen's vow, and Indra granted him the boon that named the epic's ending - rain whenever the world asked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Uttanka section (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

title.en: Sanatsujata: Death Is Not By Old Age
title.zh: 薩那特蘇鳩多：死不由於衰老

texts.period: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Sanatsujatiya), composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Udyoga Parva, Sanatsujata episode

summary.en: Dhritarashtra, terrified before the war, asked the sage Sanatsujata: is there a way past death? The answer is the epic's purest philosophy in dialogue: 'men say that by renunciation, not by rites, the wise escape death' - truth and study are the road; the fear of death is the first lie. The conversation is the Gita's dry-run in a blind king's hall.
summary.zh: 戰前惶恐的持國問仙人薩那特蘇鳩多：可有越過死亡之路？答案是史詩中最純粹的對話哲學：『人言智者以出離、而非以儀軌，脫離死亡』——真理與學習即是道路；懼死是第一個謊言。這場對話是《薄伽梵歌》在盲王之廷的預演。

passages.text: The king's question was the age's fear in one line: teach me a way beyond death; the sage's answer refused the premise - death is not escaped by rites but by knowledge.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The dialogue strips fear to its error: the fool says 'this is I'; the knower says nothing - truth, study, self-restraint; the shadow of death falls only on the one who names himself twice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Sanatsujatiya stands beside the Gita as the war's first philosophy: the same hall, the same fear, the same cure - study, taught a hundred chapters before Arjuna's chariot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

title.en: Arjuna Lays Down His Bow: The Gita's First Scene
title.zh: 阿周那放下弓：《薄伽梵歌》首景

region.en: Kurukshetra, between the two armies (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俱盧之野，兩軍之間（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva (Bhagavad Gita 1), composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Arnold translation 1885 / Ganguli 1883-96)

source.work: The Song Celestial, trans. Sir Edwin Arnold (1885), Bhagavad-Gita ch. 1

summary.en: Krishna drove the chariot to a halt between the two armies and let Arjuna see what he was about to do: grandfathers, teachers, cousins, sons-in-law on both sides. The archer of the age dropped the Gandiva from his hand and sat down in the chariot saying he would not fight - the crisis out of which the eighteen chapters of the Gita grow.
summary.zh: 克里希那御車至兩軍之間停住，令阿周那看清他將要做的事：兩邊都是祖父、教師、表親、女婿。當世第一射手垂下手中之弓，坐於車中，說他不願作戰——《薄伽梵歌》十八章由此危機而生。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (Gita recited as scripture); classified 'myth' (narrative frame rather than scripture's teaching sections).

passages.text: Krishna set the chariot before both armies and said: behold, Arjuna, what must be fought - and the hero looked at uncles and teachers and cousins arrayed to kill and be killed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Bhagavad Gita 1 (Arnold 1885); not verbatim.

passages.text: The bow slipped from his hand: his mouth dried, his body trembled, his hair stood up - I will not fight, he said; what victory buys a heap of kin?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Bhagavad Gita 1 (Arnold 1885); not verbatim.

passages.text: The despondency was the opening question of the age's philosophy: is this my dharma or my crime? - and the friend on the chariot-box began to answer as the Lord, in the conversation the whole tradition has been reading since.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Bhagavad Gita 1-2 (Arnold 1885); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Sir Edwin Arnold, The Song Celestial, 1885 (public domain)
